idea.price: Leave your seat and your chair is gone by morning, with a tail mark.
idea.title: Seat Thief
idea.twist: The law says the dragon takes a chair when its kid leaves it. Fig tapes every kid to their chair, so they are always in it, and wheels the whole class out the door.
idea.closer: Everyone here stays in their seat. We just take the seat with us.
idea.opener: In this town, every kid must stay in their seat after the final bell, or the Detention Dragon takes your chair.
idea.teaser: The rule never said the chair couldn't move.
idea.premise: At a school where chairs are guarded by a hungry dragon, a kid with a squeaky wheelie chair tries to reach the exit without moving.
examples: Mr. Plunk stood up to sneeze. Now he teaches sitting on a bucket.
The lunch lady serves soup to kids who can't get up.
Gary has been in his chair since Tuesday.
idea.narrator: Fig, the kid whose chair has wheels and cannot stay still.

idea.prop: A stale bagel in her backpack
idea.price: Last time bread was late, the pigeon announced Mr. Crumb's wig size to the whole square.
idea.title: The Polite Pigeon
idea.twist: The deal says the pigeon won't say anything 'while eating'. So Cass feeds it the stale bagel, which takes it three hours to chew, and the pigeon sits in the square chewing in total silence until the bakery opens.
idea.closer: We pay the pigeon to stay quiet. Now we just buy it the toughest bagel.
idea.opener: In this town, every night we give the Fountain Pigeon one whole loaf of bread, and it promises not to say anything.
idea.teaser: The deal said eating. The bagel said forever.
idea.premise: A town square pays a giant pigeon to keep its mouth shut about everyone's secrets, and the narrator forgets the bread one night with the mayor's secret on the line.
examples: Baker Lou bakes the loaf in the shape of a tiny hat.
The mayor tucks a note inside every loaf begging for silence.
The bus driver gives it two loaves just to be safe.
idea.narrator: Cass, who owns the town's last stale bagel and is out of fresh bread.

idea.price: A house with no soup wakes up with the chimney full of snow and the door frozen shut.
idea.title: Soup for the Yeti
idea.twist: The yeti's law says it must finish every bowl it is given, or it freezes in place. Fitz makes a giant pot of sour soup, the yeti must finish it, and it puckers and runs away for good.
idea.closer: Everyone here feeds the yeti. Now the yeti begs us to stop.
idea.opener: In this town, every family leaves one bowl of hot soup on the roof every night, for the Chimney Yeti.
idea.teaser: The yeti always finished every bowl. That was the problem.
idea.premise: Every roof in the snowy town has a bowl for the yeti, but the narrator's family only has one cursed, terrible-tasting soup recipe.
examples: Mrs. Plum sends up a soup with twelve noodles, counted.
Mr. Dobbin's soup is just warm water, and he has a frozen door.
The baker's soup is so good the pigeons moved in.
idea.narrator: Fitz, whose grandma's soup tastes like old socks and has the most sour smell in town.

idea.prop: A tin whistle in his pocket
idea.price: The last whistler's house is now a hole in the rock, and everyone has walked past it.
idea.title: Don't Whistle
idea.twist: The Worm is deaf to deep sounds but follows high whistles, so Fenn whistles his one loud note the whole way across the cave and leads the worm into the old dead tunnel while the town seals it.
idea.closer: Nobody here whistles. But when the rocks shake, they all hope I do.
idea.opener: In this town, nobody whistles in the mine tunnels, or the Rumble Worm hears and comes through the wall.
idea.teaser: The only sound it hears is the one they mocked.
idea.premise: In the underground town of Pebble Hollow, whistling is banned and the Rumble Worm is coming, but Fenn is the only kid who can't stop whistling.
examples: Baker Nell hums with her mouth stuffed with bread.
Mr. Gravel shushes the kettle before it can whistle.
The mine train honks, and only on Sundays.
idea.narrator: Fenn, who has whistled through his teeth since birth and was laughed at for it.

idea.price: Any animal that ignores a bow tie chicken gets sent to scrub the pig pen for a week.
idea.title: The Bow Tie Chickens
idea.twist: The law says anyone wearing a bow tie is boss. Pip ties a bow tie on every pig, cow and goat, so every animal is boss, and since a boss can't take orders, the chickens end up carrying the buckets themselves.
idea.closer: Only bow ties may boss the barnyard. Now everyone has one, and the chickens carry buckets.
idea.opener: In this town, only chickens with a bow tie may boss the barnyard, and every other animal must do what they say.
idea.teaser: Everyone gets a bow tie. That's the problem for the bosses.
idea.premise: On a farm, chickens in bow ties give all the orders, and Pip, a plain brown hen's kid brother, gets sick of being told to carry buckets.
examples: Bow tie Gerald ordered a cow to fetch his slippers.
The goat has been carrying one tiny chair for three days.
Farmer Hal's dog salutes every time a bow tie walks by.
idea.narrator: Pip, a farm kid with no bow tie and a pocket full of ribbon, who is stuck doing chores.

idea.price: Anyone caught bowing late has to carry a ruler's backpack to school.
idea.title: Helmet Hair Loophole
idea.twist: The law says anyone wearing a helmet rules, and it never says what kind. Beck wears a soup pot, then the whole street wears pots, mixing bowls and buckets, and everyone rules, so nobody has to bow.
idea.closer: Everyone on this street has a helmet. Mine just happens to have a handle.
idea.opener: In this town, kids with a bike helmet are Rulers of the Street, and kids with no helmet must walk and bow.
idea.teaser: The rule only said helmet. It never said which kind.
idea.premise: On Cobble Lane, helmet kids rule the sidewalks and bare-headed kids must bow, until the narrator wears something that is technically a helmet.
examples: King Marcus's helmet has a cupholder and a tiny flag.
Dolores bows so often her hat is just her spine.
The mailman salutes helmets and hands the rest their letters sideways.
idea.narrator: Beck, the only kid with no helmet, who walks, bows badly, and owns a big pot.

idea.price: Anyone caught moving when the light comes on gets eaten with the leftovers.
idea.title: The Fridge Door
idea.twist: The fridge door only opens when the light turns on. Gus sticks the magnet over the light switch, so the door stays shut forever, and the town gets to move whenever it wants.
idea.closer: We used to freeze when the door opened. Now the fridge freezes when we say so.
idea.opener: In this town, we all live inside a giant refrigerator, and every time the door opens we freeze in place.
idea.teaser: The light was the one rule they all obeyed.
idea.premise: The whole town lives among the shelves of a giant fridge, and when a hungry teenager keeps raiding it, nine-year-old Gus has to stop the door.
examples: Mrs. Butter freezes mid-sneeze every time the light turns on.
The pickle jar neighbours have practiced standing still for years.
Mr. Yogurt expired in 2019, so nobody asks him anything.
idea.narrator: Gus, the kid from the shelf of the old jam jar, who keeps a note stuck to the door with a magnet.

idea.price: Sneeze too softly and you shovel the Boomers' driveways until spring.
idea.title: The Quiet Sneezer
idea.twist: The Boomers' law says the loudest sneeze outranks all. Wren sneaks pepper to the whole shovel crowd, they sneeze together louder than any Boomer, and the law makes them the new rulers.
idea.closer: Everyone here still ranks by sneeze, but now the whole street has a cold on purpose.
idea.opener: In this town, the louder your sneeze, the higher your rank, so the Boomers sit on the snowy hilltop and everyone else sits below.
idea.teaser: The law only cares who sneezes loudest. Everyone forgot that.
idea.premise: Rank in the snowy town of Achoo Ridge is set by sneeze volume, and the narrator's sneeze is so quiet nobody has ever heard it.
examples: Mayor Gruff sneezed once and the whole bakery lost its roof snow.
Mrs. Plum sneezes in a bucket so she won't get promoted.
The mailman gets his route by sneeze, so he delivers to one house.
idea.narrator: Wren, whose sneeze is a tiny squeak, so she wears the gray shovel mittens.

idea.price: Loud dreams shake houses off their lots; the Garza garage is still crooked.
idea.title: One Left Shoe
idea.twist: The deal says one shoe, never which foot. The Sleeper, who only checks for shoes, finds Ivy's pile of right shoes and wears them proudly, and the town is saved by the exact words they always said.
idea.closer: Everyone here saves their left shoes. I saved the right ones, and that was enough.
idea.opener: In this town, every night each house leaves one left shoe on the curb for the Sidewalk Sleeper, and it promises to dream quietly.
idea.teaser: The deal says shoe. It never says which foot.
idea.premise: A suburb street pays a sleeping giant one shoe each night to keep his dreams quiet, but tonight the street has run out of left shoes.
examples: Mr. Hobb hops to work on one boot every Monday.
The twins share a single pair across two houses.
The mail truck wears a tiny sneaker on its bumper.
idea.narrator: Ivy, the kid who is the only one on the street born with two right feet.

idea.price: Anything left on the floor at lights out gets mopped into the drain.
idea.title: The Midnight Mop
idea.twist: The mop-monster mops only what is on the floor. Juno tapes every house, bed and desk up on the walls and ceiling, so the mop finds nothing and the monster gets bored and leaves.
idea.closer: In this town, we live inside a school. Now our floors are always clean, and we sleep on the ceiling.
idea.opener: In this town, we all live inside a giant school, and every night the janitor's mop bucket floods the halls.
idea.teaser: The mop only cleans what it can reach.
idea.premise: Our town lives in an enormous school building, and the mop-monster that cleans it each night is washing the town away, one hallway at a time.
examples: Mrs. Gable lost her whole kitchen table in the cafeteria once.
The Pickens twins' tricycles are somewhere under the gym.
Mr. Dunn's hat floated off to the drain last Tuesday.
idea.narrator: Juno, the smallest kid in the school-town, who keeps a roll of tape in her pocket.

idea.price: Any Stump who refuses an order has to sit on the stump all day.
idea.title: Lords and Stumps
idea.twist: The law says a Lord must obey whoever holds the antler crown. Nell hangs the crown on a Stump post, so every Lord has to obey the post, and now they all fetch her snacks.
idea.closer: Some are Lords, the rest are Stumps. Now the stump gets the last cookie.
idea.opener: In this town, kids with antlers on their heads are Lords of the Woods, and the rest of us are Stumps.
idea.teaser: The Lords' own law has a very silly loophole.
idea.premise: Antlered kids order everyone around at the woods edge, and Stump Nell wants to take her turn as Lord without any antlers of her own.
examples: Lord Barnaby makes Stumps carry his acorn collection in a wheelbarrow.
Lady Pim has a Stump to hold her umbrella.
Lord Gus demands a Stump read him bedtime stories at noon.
idea.narrator: Nell, a Stump with no antlers who keeps a very long list of rules.

idea.price: The Hendersons left one sock on the floor. By morning there was a goblin footprint and nobody had socks.
idea.title: Sock Curfew
idea.twist: The goblin sneaks in, grabs every clean sock, then sniffs Milo's gym sock on the floor. It gags and flees, dropping all the clean socks. The smell everyone teased was the one thing it can't steal.
idea.closer: In this town, every sock hides at night. Except Milo's. That one guards the whole street.
idea.opener: In this town, every sock must be in its drawer by bedtime, or the Sock Goblin takes it and the foot it came with.
idea.teaser: Everyone teases Milo's feet. The goblin can't stand them.
idea.premise: Milo's family locks every sock away at night, but Milo's socks are so stinky that they crawl out of the drawer on their own.
examples: Grandpa Fitz tapes his socks inside a cookie tin every night.
Aunt Marla counts her socks twice and sings them to sleep.
The mail carrier ties his socks to his hat before bed.
idea.narrator: Milo, whose socks are so stinky that they crawl out of every drawer.

idea.price: Anyone below the counter line eats scraps and is never allowed near the stove.
idea.title: Below the Counter
idea.twist: The rule says only kids taller than the counter may touch the stove, but it never says how they got tall. Mini climbs onto the step stool, becomes counter-height, and legally cooks the rescue meal.
idea.closer: In this town, you must be taller than the counter. I just brought my own.
idea.opener: In this town, only kids who are taller than the kitchen counter may touch the stove, so the Tall Ones run every meal.
idea.teaser: The rule only counts height. It never says how.
idea.premise: Tall kids in a giant kitchen cook, boss and eat first, while the narrator, the shortest, watches the Tall Ones promise a feast and then get trapped on the high shelf.
examples: Big Rosa stirs the soup while little kids wash the spoons.
Mr. Gable stands on tiptoes to rule the biscuit tin.
The Tall Ones sealed the cookie jar with a sign: for counter-height only.
idea.narrator: Mini, the smallest kid in the kitchen, who carries a wooden step stool.

idea.prop: a candle stub in my pocket
idea.price: Anyone without a glow gets left behind at the dark tunnel forks.
idea.title: The Bald Spot
idea.twist: At the first fork the glowing kids ran ahead, laughing. At the second they shut the gate on me. At the third they left me in the dark. Then spore fog puts every mushroom to sleep, and only my candle still lights the way home.
idea.closer: Everyone here has a glowing mushroom. But now, when the dark comes, they follow me.
idea.opener: In this town, everyone in the cave town has a glowing mushroom growing from their head, except me.
idea.teaser: When every glow goes out, the bald kid is the light.
idea.premise: Everyone in Gloamdeep lights their own way with a head-mushroom, and the one bald kid carries a plain candle stub and gets left behind at every tunnel fork.
examples: Mrs. Tuft's mushroom glows so bright she reads at bedtime.
Old Barlow's mushroom blinks blue whenever he tells a fib.
The mail carrier's mushroom is the size of an umbrella.
idea.narrator: Moss, the only bald kid in town, who carries a candle stub everywhere.

idea.price: Last time the cheese was late, the freezer door stayed open and everyone wore three sweaters.
idea.title: The Cheese Deal
idea.twist: The deal says one slice, nothing about thickness. Biscuit shaves a slice so thin you can see through it, which counts, and the fridge hums happily while the whole town's cheese lasts forever.
idea.closer: Everyone here pays one slice. Mine you can read the newspaper through.
idea.opener: In this town, every night we give the Giant Refrigerator one slice of cheese, and it promises to keep the lights on.
idea.teaser: The deal said one slice. It never said how thick.
idea.premise: Everyone lives in a giant fridge and pays cheese nightly, but this week the cheese ran out and the humming grew angry.
idea.setting: inside something giant (an animal, a store, a tower)
examples: Mr. Gouda trades slices like gold at the corner shop.
The mice union demands cheese in the morning too.
Grandma knits tiny cheese hats for the pantry cats.
idea.narrator: Biscuit, a small kid who keeps a cheese slicer and collects every crumb.

idea.price: Whatever sits under the raised flag is gone by morning.
idea.title: Raise the Flag
idea.twist: The rule says the Carrier takes only what is under the flag. Ollie tapes the flag down over the Carrier's own bag, so the Carrier takes itself away. But the flag pops up again, and a tiny shadow waves from the slot.
idea.closer: The Carrier takes whatever sits under the flag. So who raised it just now?
idea.opener: In this town, we all live inside a giant mailbox, and anything the carrier takes from the flag goes away forever.
idea.teaser: The rule only says what's under the flag. Ollie read it carefully.
idea.premise: A suburb street's families live inside a huge mailbox where the red flag marks what the Carrier will collect, and the narrator accidentally raises it over his little brother.
examples: Mrs. Lane raised the flag over her old couch and it vanished.
The Pruitts lost a whole garage sale.
Mr. Abbot's wind chimes left in the night, still ringing.
idea.narrator: Ollie, a kid who is always the last to check the flag and the first to bump into it.

idea.price: Mr. Pell stood in an aisle at closing. His mannequin tag now hangs in the window.
idea.title: After Closing Time
idea.twist: The Mannequin only grabs what stands still, so Milo wobbles and rolls on his skates through the dark aisles, and it can never catch the one thing that never holds still.
idea.closer: Everyone here learns to stand perfectly still. I am the only one who never could.
idea.opener: In this town, we all live inside a giant department store, and after closing, anyone not on a shelf belongs to the Night Mannequin.
idea.teaser: Everyone mocked how he can't stand still. Tonight that matters.
idea.premise: Our families sleep as toys on store shelves each night, but the new kid is too wobbly and keeps falling off.
idea.setting: inside something giant (an animal, a store, a tower)
examples: Mrs. Garza sleeps in the cereal aisle, holding very still beside the oats.
The Hendersons stand on the lamp shelf and pretend to be lamps.
Our mayor hides as a tall potted fern in aisle nine.
idea.narrator: Milo, who is the wobbliest kid in the store and always gets laughed at for falling over.

idea.price: Last week Captain Boots waved, and the squid shook his hand for six hours.
idea.title: Don't Wave Back
idea.twist: The squid only wanted to say hello and was lonely, because nobody ever waved first. Dot's flag starts a friendly parade, and the whole submarine learns the rule was about being brave enough to greet a friend.
idea.closer: In this town, we never wave at the squid. Except on Tuesdays, when it brings cupcakes.
idea.opener: In this town, nobody may wave at the giant squid outside the window after the bell, or it waves back with every arm.
idea.teaser: The scary squid just wants someone to say hi.
idea.premise: A submarine town stays still when the squid appears, but Dot cannot stop waving, and her waving is about to get the whole crew a very long handshake.
examples: Mr. Fizz now wears a bandage on both hands.
The cook waved once and her soup ladle got high-fived.
Cabin boy Ned was hugged by eight arms and smelled like ink.
idea.narrator: Dot, a kid who waves at everything, even the toaster.

idea.prop: A pinch of tunnel pepper in his pocket
idea.price: A big sneeze last year made the mole roll over and flatten Mr. Pogue's bakery.
idea.title: Inside the Mole
idea.twist: When the burrow floods with cold fog, nothing wakes the mole. Tuck sneezes with the pepper, the mole sits up and shakes the fog out, and the whole town cheers his giant, ridiculous sneeze.
idea.closer: Everyone in this town hates sneezing. Now they hand me pepper.
idea.opener: In this town, we all live inside a giant mole's tunnel, and every morning the walls wiggle at seven.
idea.teaser: His loudest sneeze was the town's only alarm clock.
idea.premise: A cave town lives in a huge sleepy mole's burrow, and the narrator is mocked for being the loudest sneezer in the tunnels.
examples: The mailman delivers letters by sliding them down the mole's whiskers.
Mrs. Dunn's laundry gets stuck in the mole's fur every Tuesday.
The school bus is a wheelbarrow, and it always comes late.
idea.narrator: Tuck, whose sneezes shake the walls, so everyone gives him tissues and dirty looks.

idea.price: Burp too quietly and you are moved down to the Crumb Cellar.
idea.title: The Quiet Burp
idea.twist: The Grand Belchers' law says whoever burps loudest rules, so Tilly burps into the soup can she carried everywhere, and the amplified echo shakes the cheese wheel and crowns her. Her first law: whispers rule.
idea.closer: In this town, the loudest burp rules. Now it's whoever can burp the quietest.
idea.opener: In this town, the louder your burp, the higher your rank, so the Grand Belchers rule the giant cheese wheel.
idea.teaser: The smallest burp in the cheese wheel had a secret.
idea.premise: Inside a giant cheese wheel, the loudest burpers sit on top, and the narrator can only manage a tiny polite hiccup.
idea.setting: inside something giant (an animal, a store, a tower)
examples: Mayor Gruff burps the national anthem before every meeting.
Mrs. Plum was demoted for a burp that sounded like a mouse.
The ice cream man announces himself with one long belch.
idea.narrator: Tilly, who has never burped louder than a squeaky hinge, and lives in the Crumb Cellar.

idea.prop: A slightly burnt slice of toast
idea.price: The Pickles skipped one night and woke up with their scarecrow wearing their hats.
idea.title: Likes It Best
idea.twist: Night one, Rue leaves the burnt toast, and the beast growls and the fence shakes. Night two, the barn door rattles. Night three, the beast roars at the gate, but Gary has eaten the toast first, happily, and he likes it best. The deal says the pie goes to whoever likes it best, so the beast loses and leaves forever.
idea.closer: Everyone here leaves pie for whoever likes it best. Gary says it's him.
idea.opener: In this town, every farm leaves one slice of pie on the fence post at night for whoever likes it best.
idea.teaser: Someone likes it best. Just not who they thought.
idea.premise: A farm town feeds a hungry unseen pie-eater every night, and Rue's family has no pie left, only burnt toast and a goat named Gary.
examples: Farmer Doyle bakes tractor-shaped pies for luck.
Mrs. Hen leaves her pie with a tiny fork.
The Jenkins twins eat seconds and leave only crusts.
idea.narrator: Rue, the youngest, who has only burnt toast and Gary, a goat who loves absolutely everything.

idea.price: The bowl left empty means the stump eats the porch, like the Hendersons' last winter.
idea.title: The Hungry Stump
idea.twist: The deal says the stump gets 'one bowl of soup'. Bo gives it the bowl itself, a wooden soup bowl, and the stump is fed. Now every family sends bowls, and the stump gets stuck with dishes.
idea.closer: In this town we feed the stump every night. Now we just do dishes.
idea.opener: In this town, every family leaves one bowl of soup at the woods edge, every night, for the Hungry Stump.
idea.teaser: The deal said bowl. It never said what was in it.
idea.premise: A woods-edge town feeds a giant stump each night, and the narrator's family is out of soup the one night the stump counts.
examples: Mrs. Pike leaves soup with a tiny spoon, just for manners.
Mr. Orrin sends only broth and gets his mailbox eaten.
The mayor leaves a bowl of soup the size of a bathtub.
idea.narrator: Bo, who has to deliver the bowl and accidentally has only a bowl, no soup.

idea.price: Skip the scarf and the Wind Collector takes your roof.
idea.title: The Red Scarf
idea.twist: The deal says the Wind Collector takes whatever is tied to the post by morning. Pia ties the whole town's roofs, chimneys, and the entire cliff to the post. The Wind Collector must take the post, and it leaves with it, alone.
idea.closer: Every night we tie a scarf for the wind. Now it only takes the post.
idea.opener: In this town, every night we tie one red scarf to the cliff post, for the Wind Collector.
idea.teaser: The deal says to take what is tied. Pia ties everything.
idea.premise: A cliff town ties red scarves to a post each night to pay off the Wind Collector, but the narrator's family has run out of scarves.
examples: The Bakers skipped one night. Their roof flew past the moon.
Mr. Alder ties a scarf to his hat, just in case.
The goat wears a scarf to dinner and holds it tight.
idea.narrator: Pia, the youngest of six, in charge of the scarf basket.

idea.price: Anyone who clomps after dusk gets picked up by the Hush and is never heard again.
idea.title: The Loud Shoes
idea.twist: Everyone thought the Hush took loud people. It actually hunts the silent ones, because quiet feet are its favorite food. Dot's squeak makes it back away, so the Clompers become the town's protectors.
idea.closer: Everyone here is quiet to be safe. Now they all clomp, and I lead the parade.
idea.opener: In this town, the quieter your footsteps, the higher your rank, so the Silent Steppers rule the town square.
idea.teaser: Her boots were the town's shame. Then the dark came calling.
idea.premise: Silent Steppers glide across the square in felt slippers while everyone else clomps, and the loudest kid in town keeps getting noticed by the dark.
examples: Mayor Plum has worn felt slippers since birth, even in the bath.
Mrs. Tilly got demoted for sneezing on the fountain steps.
The baker bakes bread barefoot so the oven can't hear him.
idea.narrator: Dot, whose boots squeak so loudly that she was named Clomper at birth.

idea.prop: A lumpy egg-shaped rock in her apron pocket
idea.price: A missing egg means the echo repeats everyone's embarrassing secrets all day.
idea.title: The Egg Lender
idea.twist: The rule says return 'the egg' by morning, never that it be the same egg. The echo keeps one egg and Mabel returns a rock egg, so the echo sits on it, hatching a very confused pebble.
idea.closer: In this town, we hand the Echo an egg every night. Mabel hands it a rock.
idea.opener: In this town, every night we hand one boiled egg to the Cliff Echo, and it must be returned by morning.
idea.teaser: The rule only says the egg must come back.
idea.premise: A cliff town lends an egg to a booming echo every night, and Mabel, the worst egg-boiler in town, must cook tonight's.
examples: Mr. Fennel once forgot, and the whole cliff heard his lullaby to his goat.
The baker boils eggs for forty minutes, just to be safe.
Mrs. Quill's egg came back cracked, so she wrote a complaint.
idea.narrator: Mabel, who burns water and has never boiled an egg right.

idea.price: Anyone not holding on gets tossed against the glass, and Mr. Pell still wears the dent.
idea.title: Shake Day
idea.twist: Shake one throws the baker, shake two throws Mrs. Quill, shake three lifts Wren's feet. She ties her scarf to the lamppost and tosses the end to them. The town links hands, and the shake only ever tossed people apart who weren't holding on to each other.
idea.closer: Everyone here holds on to something when the world shakes. Now I hold on to all of them.
idea.opener: In this town, we all live inside one giant snow globe, and every morning at eight someone shakes it.
idea.teaser: Every shake throws somebody. This one needs a scarf.
idea.premise: A lonely kid in a snow globe town has no one to hold on to when the daily shake comes, and today's shake is the biggest ever.
examples: The baker ties his flour sacks to the chimney every dawn.
Mrs. Quill ties a rope to her porch so her cat stays put.
Mr. Pell holds nothing, flies into the glass, and now has a dent in his hat.
idea.narrator: Wren, a kid with no family on her street, who hangs on to the lamppost alone and always wears her long red scarf.

idea.price: Ring after dark and your lamp goes out, then you do.
idea.title: The Doorbell Rule
idea.twist: The law says the Lamp Eater answers any bell that RINGS. Juno hangs clapperless bells on every door and rings them by hand. Nothing rings, so the Lamp Eater has nothing to answer.
idea.closer: Now every door here has a bell. And not one of them makes a sound.
idea.opener: In this town, every door has a bell, and anyone who rings one after dark gets answered by the Lamp Eater.
idea.teaser: The rule only says the bell must ring. Does it?
idea.premise: Deep in a cave town where every home hangs a brass bell, Juno, whose family runs the bell shop, hears a bell ring at midnight.
examples: Mrs. Tuck rang for her lost cat. Only her porch lamp came back.
The mail mole drops letters and runs before the bell can swing.
Mr. Gruff stuffs socks in his bells every single night.
idea.narrator: Juno, the bell-shop kid who is deaf in one ear and never hears the dark bells.

idea.prop: A pin from the sewing kit
idea.price: Anyone who sits below a Lord is sent to scrub the moat.
idea.title: The Pillow Lords
idea.twist: The law says whoever sits highest rules, and the pin pops every pillow tower in the hall. Everyone falls, and Dot, sitting on her bucket, is the only one still up high.
idea.closer: The law says the highest rules. Now they all call me the Bucket Queen.
idea.opener: In this town, the more cushions you sit on, the more power you have, so the Pillow Lords rule the whole castle.
idea.teaser: The law says the highest sits on top. Dot just waits.
idea.premise: The castle is ruled by those sitting on the tallest pillow towers, and a kitchen kid with a stool is the lowest of all.
examples: Lord Barnaby needs a ladder to reach his throne.
Lady Fluffington hasn't touched the floor in six years.
The court jester sits on a single pea and is ranked fourth.
idea.narrator: Dot, a kitchen kid who sits on an upside-down bucket.

idea.price: Skip the roll and your chimney goes cold until morning.
idea.title: The Fog Baker
idea.twist: The Fog Baker has been leaving perfect rolls untouched because he is too full of fine bread and craves a roll that tastes like home. Milo's burnt roll is the only one he eats, and he warms every chimney.
idea.closer: They laughed at my burnt little roll. Now the whole town fogs up for it.

Owen's shadow carries his lunch tray so he never spills.
Two shadows once swapped places at recess. Nobody has seen those kids since.
idea.narrator: Wren, the only kid at school with no shadow, who is lonely in every hallway.

idea.price: Mrs. Alder's lantern flickered out and by morning only her slippers were on the path.
idea.title: The Dark Kid
idea.twist: The Hush only takes whatever glows, because it hunts the light. Juniper covers everyone's lanterns in mud, and since the Hush cannot find anything glowing, it walks away. Her dark was the safe one.
idea.closer: Everyone here is born with light. But it was my dark that kept us safe.
idea.opener: In this town, everyone is born with a lantern on their back that glows, except me.
idea.teaser: Maybe the dark was never the danger.
idea.premise: At the woods edge, every villager carries a glowing lantern that keeps the Hush away, but I was born with a dark one.
examples: Farmer Pike polishes his lantern every sunrise.
The twins trade lantern oil like candy.
Old Wick sleeps with his lantern tied to his wrist.
idea.narrator: Juniper, the only kid in town with no lantern at all, so she hides in the shadows.

idea.price: Anyone counted twice is bundled up and gone by morning.
idea.title: The Bale Man Counts
idea.twist: The Bale Man only counts what he sees move, and he bundles any number higher than the last. Wren stacks hats on poles so he counts too many heads and bundles himself.
idea.closer: Everyone here sleeps with one head showing. Now the Bale Man sleeps in the bale.
idea.opener: In this town, we all live inside a giant hollow haystack, and every night the Bale Man counts the heads in it.
idea.teaser: He only counts. But he hates when the number is wrong.
idea.premise: A farm town lives inside one enormous haystack, and the narrator's little brother keeps sneaking out of bed after the nightly head count.
examples: Mrs. Tully sleeps under a bucket so she only counts once.
Farmer Bo ties his dog's head into a pillowcase at night.
The twins take turns sleeping so one head shows up.
idea.narrator: Wren, the only kid with two cowlicks that look like two heads from far away.

idea.price: Anyone who leaves without saying goodbye finds the bridge stretching longer every step.
idea.title: The Goodbye Bridge
idea.twist: The troll said you only leave after saying goodbye, but never said the goodbye must be to a person. Juni says goodbye to the far end, ties the yarn, and walks out as the bridge shrinks.
idea.closer: In this town, nobody leaves without saying goodbye. Juni just said it to the bridge.
idea.opener: In this town, we all live inside a giant stone bridge, and the Toll Troll lets us out only if we say goodbye first.
idea.teaser: The troll's own words left one door wide open.
idea.premise: A cliff town lives inside a bridge spanning a canyon, and the narrator must cross to fetch medicine when the troll locks every door.
examples: Postman Gus waves goodbye to forty mailboxes every morning.
Mrs. Pike takes an hour to leave the grocery store.
Kids say goodbye to their shoes before they run.
idea.narrator: Juni, who always rushes and never finishes a sentence, let alone a goodbye.

idea.price: Mr. Pickett lost both boots last winter and now hops to work.
idea.title: The Shoe Bear
idea.twist: The Stomp Bear hunts by the sound of stomping feet. Bean is so light she never makes a sound, so she tiptoes up in fuzzy slippers and returns every shoe, and the bear naps.
idea.closer: Everyone here fears the bear's ears. Now they all tiptoe, because Bean was right.
idea.opener: In this town, nobody steps past the fence of the woods after the pie bell, or the Stomp Bear takes their shoes.
idea.teaser: The bear hears every stomp. Bean has never stomped once.
idea.premise: At the woods edge, everyone obeys the pie bell curfew, but the narrator is so tiny and light that she never makes a sound when she walks.
examples: The mailman delivers in socks after six, just to be safe.
Mrs. Dobbs hid her slippers in the oven for a whole month.
The school bus now stops two miles early, and the kids hop.
idea.narrator: Bean, the smallest kid in town, who is too light to ever make a footstep sound.

idea.price: Any box left outside the truck at a stop gets tossed away for good.
idea.title: The Moving Truck Street
idea.twist: The movers' deal says all boxes marked FREE TO A GOOD HOME must be delivered. Juno's label makes the whole street official cargo that cannot be dumped, so the truck must carry everyone to a new street.
idea.closer: In this town, we all live inside a truck. And I'm the one marked free to a good home.
idea.opener: In this town, we all live inside a giant moving truck, and every street is a row of stacked boxes.
idea.teaser: One silly label turns out to matter most.
idea.premise: Our whole street rides in a giant moving truck, and when the truck's engine stops, the narrator must save every box house from the dump.
examples: Mr. Ruiz labeled his house FRAGILE, so nobody bumps his porch.
The Parks family lives under a box marked THIS SIDE UP.
Mrs. Dell hangs laundry on the tie-down straps every Tuesday.
idea.narrator: Juno, the smallest box kid, whose house is labeled FREE TO A GOOD HOME.

idea.price: Mr. Gill stepped out for a sandwich once and came back as a hat.
idea.title: Chalk Hatch
idea.twist: The Squid is afraid of smudges, because it thinks smeared chalk means a slippery trap. Fin's clumsy smears cover the whole sub and the Squid flees.
idea.closer: Everyone draws straight lines here. I'm the reason they draw them messy now.
idea.opener: In this town, every submarine hatch gets a ring of chalk, and anything outside a ring after the lights dim belongs to the Squid.
idea.teaser: The Squid fears neatness less than it fears mess.
idea.premise: Our submarine hatches are ringed in chalk to keep a hungry Squid away, and I'm the clumsy kid who always trips over everyone's rings.
examples: The captain eats his supper inside a chalk ring on his chair.
Aunt Bubbles sleeps in a ring and snores at the Squid.
The mailman delivers letters by sliding them across the line.
idea.narrator: Fin, the clumsiest kid on the sub, who smudges every chalk line she touches.

idea.price: A sneeze makes the pumpkin roll and every plate in town lands on the floor.
idea.title: The Pumpkin Patch Life
idea.twist: A sneeze rolls the pumpkin, so Milo's endless sneezes are the only thing strong enough to roll it uphill. He pepper-sneezes the whole giant pumpkin over the hill and to the barn, and the town cheers.
idea.closer: In this town we live inside a pumpkin, and Milo's sneezes are officially the town engine.
idea.opener: In this town, we all live inside a giant hollow pumpkin, and every house is a seed pocket.
idea.teaser: His sneezes ruin everything, until the one time they don't.
idea.premise: Our farm town lives in a pumpkin that rolls whenever someone sneezes, and Milo, who sneezes constantly, is blamed when a hill ahead needs climbing.
examples: Farmer Dunn eats soup only while standing on the ceiling.
The mailman glues his shoes down every morning.
Aunt Pearl keeps pillows tied to her head for rolling days.
idea.narrator: Milo, who sneezes constantly and is known as the town's wobbliest kid.

idea.price: Last time we skipped, the whale dove and the town went under.
idea.title: The Whale Won't Dive
idea.twist: The deal says feed it one lantern fish, so Marlo nets the Lantern Fish King, the whale's own guide. The whale follows its glow to a calm bay, and the whole town stays above water for good.
idea.closer: We all feed the whale one fish a night. Now it follows ours.
idea.opener: In this town, we all live inside a giant whale, and every night we feed it one lantern fish so it won't dive.
idea.teaser: The deal said one fish. It never said which.
idea.premise: A town lives inside a giant whale that must be fed a lantern fish each night, and the fisher girl catches the last one, with a storm coming.
idea.setting: inside something giant (an animal, a store, a tower)
examples: Fisher Moss rows out at dusk with his net.
Mrs. Tully keeps a lantern fish in her teapot.
The mayor counts the fish twice and still sighs.
idea.narrator: Marlo, a small fisher kid who is the only one who dares row the throat tunnel.

idea.price: The Hendersons' bulb burned out once. Their house is still there, but nobody is.
idea.title: The Promise of Light
idea.twist: The Dark promised not to come inside, so it only takes what's outside. Cleo lights her candles and goes in and shuts the door, and the Dark can't take a single step in.
idea.closer: In this town, we leave the light on for the Dark. Now we keep ourselves inside.
idea.opener: In this town, every night each house leaves its porch light on, and the Dark promises not to come inside.
idea.teaser: The promise had one small, unspoken gap.
idea.premise: Every porch light on Maple Street stays on all night for the Dark, and Cleo's bulb is the only one that keeps flickering.
examples: Mr. Gray buys bulbs by the crate and sleeps on his porch.
The Parkers have seventeen lamps for one tiny porch.
The mailman wears a headlamp and a small flag.
idea.narrator: Cleo, whose family's porch bulb is the one sad bulb that always flickers.

idea.prop: A pair of two left socks
idea.price: Skip the sock and the clock runs backward, and everyone wakes up yesterday.
idea.title: The Sock Deal
idea.twist: The deal says the goat keeps time only for 'one sock from each house.' Bea gives two left socks, so the goat must keep two times, and the clock now chimes twice as fast and the goat gets overworked and quits the deal for naps.
idea.closer: In this town, we still give the goat one sock. Now he gives us Saturdays.
idea.opener: In this town, every night we give the Clock Tower Goat one sock from each house, and it promises to keep the clock right.
idea.teaser: The goat promised one thing. Bea read the fine print.
idea.premise: Every family feeds the town's goat a single sock each night, and Bea, who owns only mismatched socks, notices the deal has a very specific wording.
examples: Mr. Pickett's clock ran backward and he ate Tuesday's breakfast twice.
The baker wears one sock so the goat gets the other.
Mayor Lump hands over a sock puppet and hopes.
idea.narrator: Bea, the only kid with two left socks, which nobody has ever offered the goat.

idea.price: Quiet sleepers sweep acorns and sleep under the porch, and everyone has seen it.
idea.title: The Snore Court
idea.twist: The judges rank by ear alone. Tuck slips earplugs to every judge, so each hears only their own snore and thinks it's the loudest. Every judge crowns themselves, then crowns Tuck too, so the ranking collapses.
idea.closer: In this town, the loudest snorer rules. Now everyone is, so nobody sweeps.
idea.opener: In this town, the loudest snore in the room outranks everyone, and quiet sleepers sweep acorns all day.
idea.teaser: Their own ears decided who was loudest. Tuck just helped.
idea.premise: Woods kids are ranked at midnight by snoring, the Loud Snorers wear leaf crowns, and one quiet sleeper has a bag of earplugs.
examples: Duke Barnaby's snore knocks birds out of the trees.
Lady Fern judges rank at midnight by ear alone.
The mayor naps inside a megaphone.
idea.narrator: Tuck, a quiet sleeper who sweeps acorns, snores like a mouse, and keeps cotton earplugs in his pocket.

idea.price: Skip the sock and the wind rips the laundry, then the bridges, then the roofs away.
idea.title: The Sock Giant
idea.twist: One dawn the rope is empty and the wind lifts the laundry, then the rope bridge, then the roofs. The giant never smells anything, so Wren's stinky sock can't be a bad smell. Its patches and holes are the only thing he can feel. He stops blowing and wears her sock, the one that feels like home.
idea.closer: Every dawn we still hang one sock. Mine is the one he asks for.
idea.opener: In this town, every dawn we hang one clean sock on the cliff rope, and the Wind Giant wears it all day.
idea.teaser: Her socks were the town's joke. Not to him.
idea.premise: A cliff town pays the Wind Giant one sock a day to keep the gusts gentle, and the narrator is the kid with the smelliest, holeiest socks.
examples: Mrs. Lark knits the socks, striped, because he is picky.
Mr. Tamm hung a soggy sock once. His roof is still missing.
The baker's twins argue over who gets sock duty.
idea.narrator: Wren, whose feet are so stinky and patched that everyone says her socks insult the giant, and the giant never smells a thing.

idea.prop: A tiny knitted cap tucked in her broom pocket
idea.price: Anyone whose hat tower falls must sit in the fountain and wave to everyone until sunset.
idea.title: The Hat Stackers
idea.twist: Biscuit tucks her tiny cap beneath the Mayor's forty hats and pulls it free. The tower tumbles, and the rule sends the Mayor to the fountain. The Stackers' towers all topple, and the fountain fills with waving rulers while Biscuit sweeps.
idea.closer: Everyone here wants the tallest hat. Now the tallest ones wave from the fountain, and I wave back.
idea.opener: In this town, the more hats you wear, the more important you are, so the Hat Stackers rule the square.
idea.teaser: One tiny cap, pulled at the right moment, topples the town.
idea.premise: In a town where rank is the height of your hat tower, Biscuit is the only Bare Head, sweeping up every hat that falls in the square.
examples: Mayor Plum wears forty hats and has not seen his own feet since spring.
Tall Mr. Gable once fell from his tower and sat in the fountain all day.
Mrs. Vance's tower has a birdhouse, and the birds pay rent.
idea.narrator: Biscuit, the only Bare Head in town, with one tiny cap and a big broom.

idea.price: Whatever crosses the stripe is carried off, like Mr. Bell's trash can, which now lives somewhere else.
idea.title: The Crosswalk Cat
idea.twist: The cat takes only what crosses the stripe, not what stays on top of it. Milo ties the hamster to the rope, lifts it by the rope above the stripe, and swings it over so it never touches. The cat blinks, bored, and the hamster is home.
idea.closer: We still never cross the stripe. But we do swing over it.
idea.opener: In this town, every sidewalk has a yellow stripe, and anything crossing it after dark belongs to the Crosswalk Cat.
idea.teaser: The cat only counts what touches the line.
idea.premise: A suburb street keeps off a giant cat's stripe at night, and the narrator's little brother has to get his hamster back from the middle of it.
examples: The mail carrier delivers by throwing from a safe distance.
Mrs. Okafor's garden gnome crossed it once. Now there's a gap.
Kids play hopscotch only on the safe side of the line.
idea.narrator: Milo, who is the best at jumping rope and the worst at following rules.

idea.price: When a clock hits zero, that person freezes like a statue until morning.
idea.title: No Clock for Me
idea.twist: The Midnight Sweeper sweeps up anyone who is frozen at zero. Dex rings the bell, and the Sweeper must obey the rule: anyone who is awake at midnight is not frozen, so it passes by the whole square and sweeps nothing.
idea.closer: In this town, everyone has a clock. Tonight, mine rang for all of them.
idea.opener: In this town, everyone in the town square has a clock over their head counting down their bedtime, except me.
idea.teaser: He can't be frozen. But everyone else can be woken.
idea.premise: Everyone's bedtime clock stops them dead at zero, and Dex, who has no clock, is the only one awake when the Midnight Sweeper arrives.
examples: Mr. Lund froze mid-sneeze next to the fountain.
The mayor froze holding a cake, and the pigeons ate it.
Mrs. Bix froze on a ladder and stayed there all night.
idea.narrator: Dex, the only kid in the square with no clock over his head.

idea.price: A small snowball means the Drift Sleeper lies down in your yard and your door freezes shut.
idea.title: The Smallest Snowball
idea.twist: The Drift Sleeper is a tiny, lonely snow creature whose paws cannot lift the big heavy balls, so it has been starving. Only Nell's marble-sized, mitten-packed snowballs fit its paws. It eats, grows warm, and melts every frozen door.
idea.closer: Everyone here brings a big snowball. Now they all roll one the size of Nell's.
idea.opener: In this town, every family leaves one snowball on the gate every night, for the Drift Sleeper.
idea.teaser: The big offerings never fit. The tiny ones always did.
idea.premise: Each night the snowy town rolls huge snowballs for the Drift Sleeper, but the narrator's hands are so small she can only roll marbles, and her mittens are all she has.
examples: Mr. Larch rolls his as big as a barrel.
The Pooles haul theirs to the gate on a sled.
Granny Wick left a lumpy one, and her door stayed frozen a week.
idea.narrator: Nell, whose hands are too small for big snowballs, but her knitted mittens pack every one hard and perfectly round.

idea.prop: A cheese rind in her pocket
idea.price: Anyone who steals another squirrel finds every acorn stolen from their roof.
idea.title: Squirrel-Free
idea.twist: The squirrels all bolt when a skunk invades. Poppy's cheese smell, the thing everyone mocked, is the only scent the skunk dislikes, so she walks it out of town as everyone follows behind her.
idea.closer: Everyone here has a squirrel. But when the skunk comes, they all stand behind my cheese.
idea.opener: In this town, everyone at the woods edge has a pet squirrel that carries their shopping, except me.
idea.teaser: Everyone has a squirrel. Nobody expected her smell to matter.
idea.premise: Every neighbour at Birchwood Edge has a loyal squirrel carrier, while Poppy hauls her groceries alone and gets mocked until a tiny, smelly problem sweeps into town.
examples: Mr. Hobb's squirrel carries his hat and his ten sandwiches.
Granny Fern's squirrel delivers her mail to the wrong porch.
The mayor's squirrel wears a tiny tie.
idea.narrator: Poppy, who has no squirrel and smells of old cheese from her pockets.

idea.price: Sir Ambrose stayed on the bridge once, and now only his helmet floats in the moat.
idea.title: The Moat Horn
idea.twist: The rule only counts the moment the horn stops. Ivy keeps blowing one long unbroken note while her brother walks off the bridge, and the dragon never sees the horn end. She stops only once he is safe on the far bank.
idea.closer: Nobody stays on the bridge when the horn stops. But the horn is mine, so I decide when it stops.
idea.opener: In this town, anyone still standing on the drawbridge when the evening horn stops is kept by the Moat Dragon.
idea.teaser: The dragon only cares when the horn stops. Ivy has a plan.
idea.premise: A castle town runs on the evening horn, and Ivy, the smallest page who blows it, sees her brother stuck on the bridge when the horn sounds early.
examples: The baker Mr. Crumb gallops his bread cart home every evening before the horn.
Lady Fenn sleeps in the gatehouse so she is never caught late.
Cook Marta counts the horn's last note out loud, then runs.
idea.narrator: Ivy, the castle's smallest page, whose only job is carrying and blowing the brass moat horn.

idea.price: No cloud means no umbrella dances, no puddles, and always the last seat at the fountain.
idea.title: Cloudless in the Square
idea.twist: A huge drought dries up the square. All the clouds are too tiny to fill the fountain. Dot's empty sky means she can stand in the middle with her bucket and catch every drip. She shares it, and the town laughs.
idea.closer: Everyone here has a cloud. But when it rains, they all stand under mine.
idea.opener: In this town, everyone has their own tiny rain cloud over their head, except me.
idea.teaser: Her clear sky is the only thing that can catch the rain.
idea.premise: Everyone in the square gets a personal weather cloud that follows them, and Dot, the one kid with nothing overhead, is laughed at during every parade.
examples: Mr. Barnaby's cloud rains on his own sandwich every day.
The mayor's thundercloud has its own tiny seat at council.
The pizza guy's cloud drizzles right into the cheese.
idea.narrator: Dot, who has a clear sky overhead and keeps a rusty old bucket, because she has nothing to dodge.

idea.price: Anyone who stomps out of rhythm wakes the bat, and a whole street was swallowed last winter.
idea.title: Inside the Bat
idea.twist: The heartbeat speeds up three times: dust falls, the lamps swing, the floor tilts. Pia drums the slow beat the town forgot, and the bat sleeps again. But her drum keeps beating after she stops, from outside the bat's wall.
idea.closer: We live inside a sleeping bat. So whose heartbeat is that outside?
idea.opener: In this town, we all live inside a giant sleeping bat, and every heartbeat shakes our cave houses.
idea.teaser: The bat is asleep again. But who is still drumming?
idea.premise: Pia has no rhythm and always stomps off the beat, yet she is the only one who can hear the bat starting to wake.
examples: Mr. Gray bakes bread only between heartbeats.
The school bell rings softly, once, in time with the pulse.
Mrs. Dunn hung her laundry from a rib. Her whole street was gone by morning.
idea.narrator: Pia, the clumsiest stomper in town, who has to drum quietly on her small wooden drum to keep time.

idea.price: A shadow that stops copying you pulls you into the lamp-dark by morning.
idea.title: The Shadow Who Waved
idea.twist: The rule says the twin must copy you exactly, so Wren draws a chalk door on the wall, steps through it, and her shadow, bound to copy, follows into the light and stays.
idea.closer: Everyone here gets a shadow-twin. Mine is late. That's why I'm still here.
idea.opener: In this town, everyone gets one shadow-twin on their tenth birthday, and it does whatever the kid does, until the first night it doesn't.
idea.teaser: Her shadow was always late. That was the clue.
idea.premise: On the town square, every ten-year-old gets a shadow-twin, and mine arrived crooked, tiny, and always a half-second late.
examples: Mrs. Fenn's twin stopped copying her once. Her porch swing still swings.
The baker's twin sneezes a second before he does now.
Old Mr. Lark keeps his lamp on all night and never sleeps.
idea.narrator: Wren, whose shadow is tiny and always lags a half-second behind her.

idea.prop: A wooden egg from the henhouse
idea.price: Skip the eggs and by morning the scarecrow stands in your garden, and your fence is gone.
idea.title: The Scarecrow's Promise
idea.twist: The deal says the scarecrow wants 'one egg from every house.' Wren leaves Biscuit's wooden egg, which counts as an egg, so it must sit on it forever and cannot walk.
idea.closer: Every night we still leave eggs. But Biscuit's is the one the scarecrow guards.
idea.opener: In this town, every night we leave one full egg basket at the barn door, and the Scarecrow promises not to walk.
idea.teaser: The promise was only as good as its wording.
idea.premise: A farm town pays a scarecrow in eggs each night to keep it standing still, and the narrator's hens just stopped laying.
examples: Mrs. Tilly forgot her basket once. Her whole pumpkin patch was moved.
The Hendersons count eggs twice, then a third time, shaking.
Farmer Grubb pays in chocolate eggs and the scarecrow still scowls.
idea.narrator: Wren, who has one stubborn hen named Biscuit that never lays anything.

idea.price: Names left off the star list are erased from the roll book by morning.
idea.title: The Chalkboard Queen
idea.twist: The Queen's deal says she erases any name 'not on the board.' Lila writes every kid's name in chalk on the board herself, so the Queen must keep them all, and the list overwhelms her until she's erased by her own rule.
idea.closer: We used to pay stars to keep our names. Now our names keep her away.
idea.opener: In this town, every kid must hand in one gold star to the Chalkboard Queen every night, or she erases a name.
idea.teaser: She wanted stars. Lila gave her every name.
idea.premise: The whole school pays gold stars to the Chalkboard Queen on the classroom board, and the narrator has none left to give.
examples: Mrs. Ames gave her last star and has no name tag.
Gus gave his star and now nobody remembers his birthday.
The janitor hands in a star every night, grumbling.
idea.narrator: Lila, who has no gold stars because she always forgets her homework.

idea.price: Anyone still on the slide when the flag rises is delivered far away.
idea.title: The Slow Letter
idea.twist: The mailman only picks up what moves fast, so Rosie, slow as always, is overlooked, and her slow wind-up snail marches the whole street out of sight until the flag falls and everyone is safe.
idea.closer: They laughed that I was slow. Now the whole street walks like me.
idea.opener: In this town, we all live inside a giant mailbox, and every house is a letter slot that opens at noon.
idea.teaser: The slowest kid on the street saves everyone.
idea.premise: Everyone in the mailbox town zips through their slot at noon, but Rosie is slow, and the day the flag goes up, the mailman is about to lift the whole street away.
examples: Mr. Ames got delivered to the next county last spring.
The Hendersons mail their lunches ahead each morning.
Our paper boy lives permanently in the dead letter bin.
idea.narrator: Rosie, the slowest kid on the street, who always gets teased for walking at a snail's pace.

idea.price: Footprints in fresh snow at dawn, stitched shut, and the walker never seen again.
idea.title: The Stitcher's Needle
idea.twist: The Stitcher only sews footprints it finds. Wren walks backward in her own tracks, then snips the thread at the end, so no footprints are left to stitch and it stitches itself shut.
idea.closer: Nobody walks on fresh snow after dark here. Except the one who leaves no footprints.
idea.opener: In this town, nobody walks on fresh snow after dark, or the Snow Stitcher sews your footprints shut with you inside.
idea.teaser: The rule says footprints. It never says whose.
idea.premise: Everyone in a snowy town sticks to shoveled paths at night, but the shovel-less kid next door has to cross a fresh white yard to fetch her brother's lost mitten.
examples: Mr. Hanley's boots still stand in the yard, stitched into the drift.
The mail carrier only delivers along the shoveled gray stripe.
Mrs. Okoro's dog walks on a plank, and it never complains.
idea.narrator: Wren, the kid whose family can't afford a shovel, so her path is always snow.

idea.price: A crystal that goes dark means that person is sealed into the rock by morning.
idea.title: The Blank Crystal
idea.twist: The Sealing Rule says anyone whose name goes dark is sealed. Nell's crystal has no name, so it can never go dark. She chalks the sealed names back on, and the rock lets everyone out.
idea.closer: Everyone here has a name on the wall. I'm the only one the dark can't write.
idea.opener: In this town, everyone's name is carved into a glowing crystal in the cave wall, except mine.
idea.teaser: Nobody guessed that having no name could be a loophole.
idea.premise: In a cave town where every crystal name keeps its owner's light on, the narrator is the only kid whose crystal is smooth and has no name at all.
examples: Mrs. Tilly polishes her crystal every dawn before she touches her breakfast.
Mr. Grubb's crystal flickered once. His whole family sat watching it all night.
The baker sells bread shaped like crystals, with names written in icing.
idea.narrator: Nell, the only kid whose crystal has no name, so the town says she has no light.

idea.price: A hum that clashes with the bell cracks the rock, and the cracked houses fall.
idea.title: The Bell Town
idea.twist: A storm wind cracks the bell and the town's ringing goes silent and flat. Only Wren's off-key kazoo hum fits the crack's pitch and shakes the stuck stones loose, so the bell sings whole again.
idea.closer: In this town, we all live inside a bell, and now we ring a little off-key.
idea.opener: In this town, we all live inside a giant hollow cliff-top bell, and the whole town rings when the wind blows.
idea.teaser: Everyone told her to hum quieter. The bell disagreed.
idea.premise: A town lives inside a huge stone bell on a cliff, and the one kid who cannot stop humming is told to be quiet.
examples: Mrs. Tilly bakes bread only when the wind is calm.
Mr. Ferris ties pillows to his boots every morning.
The mailman delivers letters by walking on tiptoe.
idea.narrator: Wren, who hums off-key all day and gets shushed by everyone.

idea.price: A cold or empty cup means a porch light goes dark by morning.
idea.title: One Cup for the Hush
idea.twist: The rule says leave a cup of cocoa 'on the porch, for the Hush.' Juno leaves the cup on the Hush's own porch at the end of the street, so it must drink from its own cup and go home.
idea.closer: Every family leaves one cup on the porch. Mine is on yours, Hush.
idea.opener: In this town, every family leaves one cup of cocoa on the porch at night, for the Hush.
idea.teaser: The deal said porch. It never said whose.
idea.premise: Every night the Hush drinks the cocoa left on porches, and the narrator's family has just run out of cocoa and got a deal wrong.
examples: Mr. Vance left milk once. His porch is still dark.
The Pruitts leave two cups, just to be safe.
Mrs. Abara stirs hers clockwise, for manners.
idea.narrator: Juno, who has to put out the cup tonight because Dad is away.

idea.price: Anyone left on the ground at dark is gone by morning, leaving only their boots.
idea.title: The Last Ladder
idea.twist: The serpent hates loud metal, which is why the bell-ringer and Sir Bram were never taken. Tilly clangs across the drawbridge, the serpent shrinks into the moat, and she carries her brother home.
idea.closer: Everyone here climbs the ladder. But when I walk, the serpent hides.
idea.opener: In this town, every tower window drops a rope ladder at sunset, and anything left on the ground belongs to the Moat Serpent.
idea.teaser: Everyone teased her braces for clanking. The serpent heard them differently.
idea.premise: The castle town climbs ladders every night to escape the serpent, but Tilly, the slowest kid, cannot climb, and her little brother is stuck outside the wall.
examples: Baker Wend left his cart out and found only wheels.
The bell-ringer clangs his bell all night and is always fine.
Sir Bram clanked home late in armor, and the serpent slid away.
idea.narrator: Tilly, the smallest kid in the castle, with heavy metal leg braces that clank and can't climb a ladder.

idea.price: Skip a drawing and the wall eats that kid's name off the roll sheet.
idea.title: The Hungry Mural

idea.closer: Everyone here draws perfect pictures. But the wall only ever asks for mine.
idea.opener: In this town, every kid leaves one crayon drawing in the lunchroom cubby every night, for the Hungry Mural.
idea.teaser: The wall is hungry, but not for perfect.
idea.premise: A school feeds a blank wall its best drawings every night, and the narrator draws so badly that nobody wants to be her partner.
examples: Mrs. Tubbs draws a perfect rainbow each night, shaded and framed.
Dex traced a dog once, and the mural spat it back.
The twins draw together so nobody can say who skipped.
idea.narrator: Juniper, who draws wobbly stick people and gets laughed at in art class.

idea.prop: A pair of thin, patched slippers
idea.price: Anyone who steps on the high bridge too heavily falls into the canyon mist.
idea.title: Light Feet
idea.twist: The old rope bridge is too fragile for any heavy boots, so the Stompers cannot cross to save the stranded children on the far cliff. Wren tiptoes across in her light slippers, ties the rope tight, and leads everyone over.
idea.closer: Up here, heavy boots rule. Down here, the lightest feet carry us all home.
idea.opener: In this town, the heavier your boots, the higher your cliff ledge, so the Stompers rule the top.
idea.teaser: Only the lightest feet can cross the broken bridge.
idea.premise: A canyon town ranks everyone by boot weight, and the narrator wears featherlight shoes at the bottom when the bridge begins to crack.
examples: Baron Clump wears boots made of anvils.
Mrs. Pebble needs three people to lift her shoe.
The mail goat carries lead in its saddlebags.
idea.narrator: Wren, the lightest kid in the canyon, who wears paper-thin slippers and gets laughed at.

idea.price: Anyone who wakes the bear gets their house shaken loose and dropped in the snow.
idea.title: Inside the Bear
idea.twist: Spring comes and the bear stirs too early, and every loud voice makes it grumble. Only Pim's feather tickle is soft enough to ease it back to sleep, and the quiet kid saves the town.
idea.closer: Everyone here is loud. But now, when the bear stirs, they all look for me.
idea.opener: In this town, we all live inside a giant sleeping bear, and the loudest snore of the year is our alarm clock.
idea.teaser: Nobody could shout loud enough. Except the quietest kid.
idea.premise: A town lives in a hibernating bear's fur, and the narrator is the smallest, quietest kid, teased for never being heard.
idea.setting: inside something giant (an animal, a store, a tower)
examples: Mrs. Birch hangs laundry on the bear's whiskers.
Big Otto stomps and the whole town gets sent to the floor.
The mailman delivers letters along the left ear ridge.
idea.narrator: Pim, the smallest and quietest kid, who the town jokes about as barely there.

idea.price: Kids whose shadows wander off get lost in the fog and sleep in the canyon.
idea.title: The Shadowless Kid

idea.closer: Everyone here has a shadow to follow. But when it's foggy, they follow me.
idea.opener: In this town, everyone on the cliff has a long shadow that walks ahead of them, except me.
idea.teaser: When the fog came, the shadows all disappeared. Except nothing changed for Fen.
idea.premise: On a cliff town where shadows guide everyone down the zigzag stairs, the narrator has no shadow and is laughed at and left behind each morning.
examples: Mr. Tuck's shadow leads him straight to the bakery every dawn.
The mail carrier follows hers along the ledge like a dog.
Twins Ida and Ozzie hold shadow hands to cross the bridge.
idea.narrator: Fen, who has no shadow at all, and is called Noon because of it.

idea.prop: A little jam jar with holes
idea.price: Kids with no fireflies get moved one row farther from the lantern ring each night.
idea.title: The Dark Kid
idea.twist: Night one Wren is pushed to the back row, night two to the fence, night three outside the ring. She sets her jar open on a stump. One dim, tired firefly moves in, then brings its whole family, because fireflies follow kids who give them a home.
idea.closer: Everyone here counts fireflies. Now they count how many of them sleep in my jar.
idea.opener: In this town, the more fireflies follow you home, the more important you are, so the Glowers rule the woods edge.
idea.teaser: Nobody follows Wren. Somebody's about to move in.
idea.premise: At the woods edge, rank is counted in fireflies, and Wren, who attracts none and secretly keeps a jam jar, gets pushed farther back every night.
examples: Mayor Tilly wears a cloud of fireflies like a fluffy hat.
The Glowers get front-row seats at the pancake breakfast.
Mr. Burrow has forty fireflies and has never carried his own bag.
idea.narrator: Wren, who has zero fireflies and secretly keeps an old jam jar with holes in her coat pocket.

idea.prop: A notebook and a pencil stub
idea.price: Speak a wish after noon and your voice is gone by sunset.
idea.title: The Echo Square
idea.twist: The rule says 'speak a wish out loud', so I write the town's wishes in the notebook and read them in silent sign. The Echo has no claim on written words and must hand every voice back.
idea.closer: In this town, nobody speaks a wish after noon. We write them, and they all come true.
