idea.teaser: The Echo took every voice, but it forgot how the rule was worded.
idea.premise: The square's fountain goes silent each noon, and when the Echo takes my brother's voice, I have to rescue the whole town using only the exact words of the rule.
examples: Baker Odd wished for more customers and now only waves.
Mayor Plum wished for a longer lunch and now whispers on paper.
The twins wished for snow and now only sign to each other.
idea.narrator: A kid who always writes instead of talks, so the Echo has nothing to take from me.

idea.price: Anyone who stands in the light when the door opens is picked up and gone.
idea.title: The Fridge Light
idea.twist: The Giant's own rule on the note says he only takes food that is not labeled. Dot labels every house, shelf and neighbor with a sticky tag reading 'leftovers, do not eat', and the door closes empty-handed.
idea.closer: The light only takes what's unlabeled. So we labeled everything, even the dark.
idea.opener: In this town, every house on Elm Street sits inside one giant refrigerator, and when the door opens, the light means someone is hungry.
idea.teaser: The Giant follows one rule. Dot just reads it carefully.
idea.premise: The families of Elm Street live on the shelves of a giant refrigerator, and Dot hears the door open at night.
examples: Mr. Gable's cheese house was gone the morning after the midnight snack.
The Ortiz family keeps a rule: never stand on the top shelf.
Our mail goes by egg carton so nobody walks in the light.
idea.narrator: Dot, a kid who lives in the butter dish and keeps a deal slip from the hungry Giant.

idea.price: The Pickups left a single shoe in the street the night the Hendersons stayed out.
idea.title: Lid Closes at Nine
idea.twist: The rule says anything outside the can goes in the trash. Milo drags the whole neighborhood's trash outside, and the lid, following its own words, takes the trash instead of the people.
idea.closer: In this town, we live inside a garbage can, and the lid took only the trash.
idea.opener: In this town, we all live inside a giant garbage can, and the lid closes every night at nine.
idea.teaser: The lid takes what's outside. So what's outside?
idea.premise: Our suburb street sits inside a giant garbage can, and at nine the lid slams shut, and anyone outside at dark gets taken out with the trash.
examples: Mr. Cobb's dog barks at the lid every dusk.
The paperboy sprints home before eight forty.
Mrs. Vale keeps her curtains stitched shut.
idea.narrator: Milo, who always runs late because his sneakers are a size too big.

idea.price: Yesterday the Collector took Mr. Dunn's shadowless cousin, and only his hat stayed on the bench.
idea.title: No Guard Shadow
idea.twist: The Collector's law is that it takes only what has no shadow. Ivy shines her flashlight on the Collector itself, so it casts no shadow, and it takes itself away at dawn.
idea.closer: Everyone here has a shadow. But now when the Collector comes, they all call me.
idea.opener: In this town, everyone in the town square has a lantern shadow that stands guard over them, except me.
idea.teaser: The Collector takes anyone without a shadow. Does it have one?
idea.premise: Every person in the square has a tall guardian shadow, and the narrator's shadow is missing just as the Dusk Collector begins taking shadowless people.
examples: Baker Rosa's shadow kneads dough in the dark.
The mayor's shadow stands taller than the clock tower.
Little Wes has a shadow that only waves at pigeons.
idea.narrator: Ivy, who has no shadow and keeps a flashlight in her coat pocket.

idea.price: The one night a bowl was forgotten, the lamps went out for a week.
idea.title: Soup for the Deep
idea.twist: The Deep One is not a beast but a giant, lonely mole who keeps the town's lamps lit with its glow, and the soup is the only company it has. Odie sits down and eats with it, and now every night a kid comes to dinner.
idea.closer: Every night this town sends down soup. But now, somebody finally sends down a kid to eat it.
idea.opener: In this town, every family lowers one warm bowl of soup down the old mine shaft every night, for the Deep One.
idea.teaser: Someone down there is as lonely as he is.
idea.premise: In a cave town that feeds something below the mine, lonely Odie decides to follow his soup bowl down the shaft one night to see who is really eating.
examples: Mrs. Gritt adds extra pepper so the Deep One sneezes.
The Tanner twins lower theirs with a tiny rope elevator.
Old Mr. Cobb once sent down a bowl of cold beans, and the town shook.
idea.narrator: Odie, a lonely cave kid whose parents work late and who eats dinner by himself.

idea.price: Any room that drifts too far from the castle wall gets eaten by the Moat Frog.
idea.title: The Lily Pad Castle
idea.twist: Fig's yarn ties her pad to every other pad, and the Moat Frog only eats rooms that drift alone. The rule was never about distance. It was about being tied to someone, and nobody is ever lonely again.
idea.closer: Everyone here lives on a lily pad. Now we all float tied together.
idea.opener: In this town, we all live inside a giant castle moat, and every room is a floating lily pad.
idea.teaser: The frog only ever wanted one thing from the lily pads.
idea.premise: A whole castle town lives on floating lily pad rooms in the moat, and the narrator's pad is the smallest and keeps drifting away.
examples: Mr. Gable's bedroom drifted to the drawbridge, and he now commutes by catapult.
The school bus is a duck, and it only goes where it wants.
Mrs. Tully ties her kitchen to her neighbor's with a long spaghetti noodle.
idea.narrator: Fig, whose tiny lily pad room drifts away every night.

idea.price: Skip the bread once and the windmill's shadow eats the whole cornfield by morning.
idea.title: Bread for the Grinder
idea.twist: Wren wears the mitt to open the windmill door and finds the Grinder is a lonely old machine that mills the bread into flour, which it secretly sends back as the town's morning loaves. It was feeding them all along.
idea.closer: Everyone here feeds the monster. Turns out, it was feeding us, and now I have a family at its table.
idea.opener: In this town, every family carries one warm loaf of bread to the old windmill every night, for the Grinder.
idea.teaser: Everyone feeds the monster. Nobody asks where the bread goes.
idea.premise: Farm families feed the creaking windmill monster each night, and the lonely kid with no family on the farm is the only one who ever stays to listen.
examples: Mrs. Tully bakes twelve loaves, just in case her cat gets hungry.
Farmer Boggs once brought stale bread and lost every pumpkin.
The Hendry twins deliver theirs on a skateboard, very fast and very scared.
idea.narrator: Wren, the orphan farmhand who has no family to bake for, only a borrowed oven mitt.

idea.price: A house with no blanket on the rope wakes to a cold, empty porch.
idea.title: The Blanket Rope
idea.twist: The Thing is a lost, shivering creature that was cold, not hungry, and Eli has been looking after it. Tuck's red scarf finds him, and now the town sends blankets with a letter inside.
idea.closer: We send a blanket every night. Now we send a letter to my brother too.
idea.opener: In this town, every night each cliff house sends one warm blanket down the rope to the Thing in the canyon.
idea.teaser: Tuck climbs down to find out what the blankets are for.
idea.premise: A cliff town lowers blankets into the dark canyon every night, and Tuck, who lost his brother there, decides to follow the rope down.
examples: Mrs. Hale knits her blanket in the shape of a sheep.
The mayor sends a blanket with a tiny crown on it.
Mr. Dunn once sent a doormat, and his porch vanished.
idea.narrator: Tuck, whose big brother Eli went down the rope last winter and never came back.

idea.price: Mr. Ferris left his ladder out once. By morning his whole porch was gone.
idea.title: Roll Up the Bridges
idea.twist: The Gap only takes what is on a ledge with no bridge. Juno ties the rope between the two ledges and rolls it up with her brother on it. He is on a bridge, not a ledge, so the Gap has no claim.
idea.closer: We still roll up the bridges at sundown. But now one stays unrolled for anyone who's late.
idea.opener: In this town, every rope bridge is rolled up at sundown, and anyone still on a ledge belongs to the Gap.
idea.teaser: The rule says ledges only. Juno finds something that isn't one.
idea.premise: A cliff town rolls up its bridges every night, and the narrator's little brother is stuck on the far ledge when the sun drops.
examples: The mail carrier sprints the last bridge every day at five.
Mrs. Lund keeps a snack bag on both ledges, just in case.
The Tuttle twins got stuck out there once and never came home.
idea.narrator: Juno, the bridge-roller's kid, who knows every knot on every rope.

idea.price: Old Mr. Bolt's cat sat in the window after the bell. By morning only the cushion was left.
idea.title: The Watcher
idea.twist: The Watcher takes only what it sees, so Otis, laughed at all week, switches on his flashlight and shines it into the huge eye. All it sees is white light, so it takes the light and leaves the town alone forever.
idea.closer: In this town, we cover the portholes at the bell. Except one, and that one watches back.
idea.opener: In this town, when the bell rings, every porthole gets covered, or the Watcher takes whatever it sees through.
idea.teaser: It takes whatever it sees. So Otis shows it something.
idea.premise: In a sunken sub town, one porthole stays uncovered at the bell, and a huge round eye drifts toward the glass.
examples: Mrs. Reef sews porthole curtains in every size, even for the toaster.
The sub cook stuffs socks over the kitchen porthole.
Twins Kip and Lou keep their eyes closed after the bell.
idea.narrator: Otis, the lamp boy, whose habit of carrying a flashlight everywhere gets laughed at by every neighbour.

idea.price: Anyone caught without light after the bell is gone by morning, leaving an empty cot.
idea.title: The Candle Line
idea.twist: Wick melts the stubs into one big wax lump and lights it at the stairs. The dark backs off and every cellar kid climbs up. Then he counts them: one more than went down.
idea.closer: Keepers sleep upstairs, the rest of us sleep downstairs, and now someone sleeps between.
idea.opener: In this town, kids who own a candle are Keepers who sleep upstairs, and kids without one sleep in the dark cellar halls.
idea.teaser: He won the light. Then he counted the kids.
idea.premise: In a castle split by a staircase, Wick has no candle, sleeps in the cellar halls, and notices the dark down there keeps counting heads.
examples: Lady Pim's candle is so tall she needs a ladder.
Cook Barrow lost his stub once and his cot stayed empty.
The Keepers line the stairs with flames so we can't climb.
idea.narrator: Wick, a cellar kid with no candle who has to feel his way along the walls.

idea.prop: A paper sign reading ASK FIRST
idea.price: Anyone who breaks a house rule is vacuumed into the hall closet until dinner.
idea.title: Grounded Rules
idea.twist: The Vacuum must obey every house rule. Ollie holds up his sign, so the Vacuum has to ask before it enters the living room. It never learned to talk, so it stays out forever.
idea.closer: Everyone here makes a house rule. But the Vacuum only follows mine.
idea.opener: In this town, everyone gets one house rule the first time they get grounded, and the whole house must obey it.
idea.teaser: His rule sounds boring. The Vacuum has to follow it.
idea.premise: Kids in the Parker house make a rule when grounded, but Ollie's rule seems useless while a giant vacuum hungrily sucks up every toy in the living room.
examples: Dad's rule is that nobody touches the thermostat.
Big sister Jo banned socks on the kitchen floor.
Grandma's rule is that dessert comes first.
idea.narrator: Ollie, whose rule is that nobody may enter the living room without asking.

idea.price: Step on the carpet and you're in detention until report card day.
idea.title: Hall Monitor Moose
idea.twist: The Moose hears only silence as safe, and everyone who tiptoes is easy to catch. Pib's squeaky shoes squeak so loud the Moose thinks it's a bugle and marches out proudly.
idea.closer: In this town nobody steps off the tile. Now the Moose salutes my shoes.
idea.opener: In this town, nobody steps off the hallway tiles after the last bell, or the Hall Monitor Moose carries you to detention.
idea.teaser: Everyone tiptoed. Pib squeaked.
idea.premise: After the last bell, a giant moose patrols the school halls, and the narrator is stuck on the wrong side with squeaky shoes.
examples: Mr. Fenn hopped on one tile for a whole hour.
The lunch ladies roll their carts on the grout lines.
Brenda wears slippers to sneak, and still got caught.
idea.narrator: Pib, the kid with the loudest squeaky shoes in school.

idea.prop: Her tin spoon for tapping pebbles
idea.price: Skip a night and every lamp in the tunnels goes dark until morning.
idea.title: The Drum Bucket
idea.twist: The deal says the Drum gets one bucket of echoes, not pebbles. Wren taps her tin spoon against the walls and fills the bucket with echoes. The Drum rumbles happily and the lights return, and the town never needs pebbles again.
idea.closer: Every night we give the Drum a bucket. Wren just fills it with a spoon.
idea.opener: In this town, every night we give the Deep Drum one bucket of echo pebbles, or it stops the cave lights.
idea.teaser: The bucket is empty. The cave is not.
idea.premise: The cave town of Echo Hollow pays a bucket of pebbles to the Deep Drum each night, and tonight the town has run out.
examples: Mr. Hobb counts pebbles out loud and still loses three.
The baker pays in tiny crumb-sized pebbles and gets scolded.
Twins Pia and Pim polish every pebble till it shines.
idea.narrator: Wren, the pebble carrier's kid, who is too small to lift a full bucket.

idea.price: Anyone squeaky enough gets sucked into the vacuum's hallway for the night.
idea.title: Silent Socks
idea.twist: The vacuum only hunts squeaks, and the Squeakers can't hide. Mo's silent socks are the only way across the carpet unnoticed, so he sneaks to the plug and pulls it, saving everyone.
idea.closer: Everyone here ranks by squeak. Now they all beg me for quiet.
idea.opener: In this town, the louder your socks squeak, the higher your rank, so the Squeakers rule the living room.
idea.teaser: The thing they mocked is the only thing the vacuum can't hear.
idea.premise: In a living room ruled by squeaky socks, the narrator wears the quietest pair, which everyone mocks, until a giant vacuum starts hunting for squeaks.
examples: Lord Dennis squeaks so loudly the cat hides under the couch.
The royal guards polish their socks with olive oil.
Aunt Priya tiptoes just to avoid being promoted.
idea.narrator: Mo, whose silent socks have never squeaked once and get mocked daily.

idea.price: Skaters who touch bare snow get stuck there until spring.
idea.title: The Boy Who Walks
idea.twist: The rule says skaters get stuck on bare snow, but Tuck's plain feet never stick. He walks across the powder, ties the rope to the stuck skaters, and hauls the entire town to the glass lake.
idea.closer: Everyone here has skates. But now, when the snow gets deep, they call me.
idea.opener: In this town, everyone is born with a pair of ice skates frozen to their feet, except me.
idea.teaser: Everyone glides. Only one kid can walk to them.
idea.premise: In a snowy town where everyone glides on built-in skates, one boy has plain feet, and a blizzard strands the whole town's skaters on the glass lake.
examples: Mrs. Lund skated to church and got stuck in a drift until April.
The mailman glides everywhere but can't stop, so he waves while passing.
Mr. Brisk skated onto the soft powder and became a snowman's neighbor all winter.
idea.narrator: Tuck, the only kid with ordinary feet, who plods while everyone else glides.

idea.price: The Parker kids said goodnight once. By morning their bedroom lights were taped dark and their beds were tucked in tight with nobody inside.
idea.title: Don't Say Goodnight
idea.twist: The rule says out loud, so Rue tapes the toaster's goodnight shut, covering its lever and the word on its label. She then writes goodnight on a note and tapes it to the door. The Dim Man finds only silence and a written word, and leaves at sunrise.
idea.closer: Nobody here says goodnight after nine. But a note on my wall says it for me.
idea.opener: In this town, nobody says goodnight out loud after the kitchen clock strikes nine, or the Dim Man comes to tuck you in.
idea.teaser: She found a way to say it without saying it.
idea.premise: Every house goes quiet at nine, but Rue's little brother loves saying goodnight to everything and has just whispered it to the toaster.
examples: Mr. Finch nods at his wife and winks instead.
The Parker twins use a flashlight code for bedtime.
Even the parrot at number nine wears a tiny muzzle after dark.
idea.narrator: Rue, who talks in her sleep and always says goodnight to everybody.

idea.prop: A red thread knotted on his wrist
idea.price: Any sock left unmatched on laundry day is carried off in the big hand, like Mr. Wooly's cousin last week.
idea.title: Laundry Day
idea.twist: The big hand only grabs socks that aren't tied to anything. Moss ties his red thread to a neighbour, and everyone ties on, so the drawer is one linked chain. The hand can't pick out any single sock, so it leaves.
idea.closer: In this town, we all live in a sock drawer. And nobody is ever left without a match.
idea.opener: In this town, we all live inside one giant sock drawer, and laundry day comes every Sunday.
idea.teaser: Moss has no match. The whole drawer is about to change that.
idea.premise: A family of tiny neighbours lives in the sock drawer, and Moss, the loneliest kid, has no matching sock to call a friend as Sunday nears.
examples: Mrs. Argyle sold buttons until the big hand took her unmatched neighbour.
The Stripe brothers race along the drawer track, always side by side.
Mr. Wooly pairs up with his twin before every Sunday.
idea.narrator: Moss, the one lonely sock-kid whose pair was lost in the dryer.

idea.prop: A tiny sign reading 'Please say thank you'
idea.price: Last time the soup was late, every fountain in town turned to pudding.
idea.title: The Rude Statue
idea.twist: The statue's deal says it will protect the town as long as it's thanked for the soup. Pearl puts her sign in front of it, and since it never says thank you, the deal turns against it and it must serve the soup back.
idea.closer: We feed the statue every night. Now it brings us soup on Tuesdays.
idea.opener: In this town, every night we serve one bowl of soup to the statue in the square, who never says thank you.
idea.teaser: The statue never said thank you. Pearl noticed.
idea.premise: A stone statue in the town square gets a hot bowl of soup nightly, and nobody has ever heard it say thank you, which makes me furious.
examples: Mayor Plum stirs the soup with his hat on.
The baker adds extra croutons to be polite.
Little Jo Pickett once forgot the spoon and the fountain wobbled.
idea.narrator: Pearl, a kid who gets in trouble for correcting everyone's manners.

idea.prop: a folded ticket to the desert
idea.price: Anyone whose cloud melts completely must move to the sunny desert village forever.
idea.title: Cloudless in the Snow
idea.twist: The rule says anyone whose cloud melts must leave, but Bix never had a cloud, so he can never melt. The mayor tries to send him away with the ticket, and the loophole means Bix is the only one who gets to stay. He picks everyone's ice cream flavor.
idea.closer: In this town, everyone has a cloud, except me, and that's why I'm staying.
idea.opener: In this town, everyone has a tiny weather cloud of snow above their head that says how cold they are, except me.
idea.teaser: The rule only counts clouds that exist.
idea.premise: Everyone in the snowy town has a personal snow cloud that shows their mood, but Bix has a plain empty sky above him and gets teased constantly.
examples: Mr. Gruff has a blizzard, so his mailbox is permanently buried.
Mrs. Sleet's cloud sneezes flakes into the soup.
The mayor's cloud is so small it needs a tiny scarf.
idea.narrator: Bix, who has no cloud at all and a pocket full of tickets nobody wants.

idea.price: Any kid who skips the offering finds their lunchbox empty and their desk gone by morning.
idea.title: Homework for the Lunch Lady
idea.twist: The deal says the Lunch Lady keeps whoever's homework is not finished. Milo slides in his blank page; she must keep a blank homework, which is no kid at all, and she lets his sister go, bound by her own words.
idea.closer: In this town, we feed the Lunch Lady homework. Now she only eats what's finished, and I'm still not finished.
idea.opener: In this town, every kid slides their homework under the cafeteria door every night, for the Lunch Lady who never sleeps.
idea.teaser: The deal says homework. It never says whose.
idea.premise: Every night the school feeds the unseen Lunch Lady our homework, and when Milo's little sister's math sheet is accidentally taken, the Lunch Lady promises to keep her until it's done.
examples: Mr. Finch hands in his crossword every single night.
Penny once slid in a spelling test with her name misspelled.
The principal feeds her a stack of permission slips every Friday.
idea.narrator: Milo, a kid who never finishes homework and still owns one blank page from the first day.

idea.price: When the Cook missed a pie, the bakery's roof was found hanging off the cliff.
idea.title: The Canyon Cook's Deal
idea.twist: The deal says the Cook never eats the town, but it never says the Cook can't eat pies off the town. Fig rewrites the deal so the Cook only eats pie, and the town gets a free cook.
idea.closer: In this town, we lower one pie every night. The Cook now sends back a thank-you note.
idea.opener: In this town, every night we lower one pie on a rope to the Canyon Cook, who promises never to eat the town.
idea.teaser: The deal had exactly one rule. Fig read the rest.
idea.premise: The cliff town lowers pies nightly into the canyon to appease a hungry cook, but tonight the baker burns the pie and the narrator's bargaining begins.
examples: Mr. Tuck bakes the pie while wearing oven mitts on his ears.
The mayor tastes every pie first, for safety and for himself.
Granny Pell sends the pies down with a note full of compliments.
idea.narrator: Fig, the baker's kid, who reads every contract and always carries a pencil.

idea.price: The shadowless who cross the porch vanish into the white, leaving only boots in the snow.
idea.title: Shadowless
idea.twist: The Frost King promised that no shadowless child would leave unharmed, but never said she could not carry a light. Wren's lantern casts her a shadow, and everyone's shadows follow her instead.
idea.closer: They said the shadowless can't walk outside. They never said I couldn't bring the light.
idea.opener: In this town, only kids who own a snow shadow may walk outside, and the shadowless must stay behind the frosted windows.
idea.teaser: No shadow, no rules. Unless she makes her own.
idea.premise: Shadow-kids play outside while shadowless kids watch from windows, and the narrator sneaks out, hunting for the brother whose shadow was taken last winter.
examples: Mr. Fenn's shadow shovels his driveway while he drinks cocoa.
The mail shadow delivers letters and the mailman waves from inside.
Granny Pell's shadow does her knitting, badly.
idea.narrator: Wren, born with no shadow, who has watched the street through frost for ten winters.

idea.price: Kids who wished big were gone by morning, with only their shoes left at the treeline.
idea.title: The Whispering Wish
idea.twist: The trees grant wishes word for word, and take the wisher to fit the wish. Moss wished for the blanket to keep everyone warm, and the trees must wrap everyone, so the taken kids come home wrapped in it.
idea.closer: In this town, everyone gets a wish. Mine was small, so everyone came back.
idea.opener: In this town, everyone gets one wish granted the first night they hear the woods whisper their name.
idea.teaser: The trees always give exactly what you say.
idea.premise: Every kid at the woods edge gets a wish from the whispering trees, and Moss, who wished for a warm blanket, is the only one still home.
examples: Tommy wished to be tall. His shoes are still at the treeline.
Mrs. Park wished for endless cookies. Her kitchen is empty.
Dara wished for a thousand friends. Now the trees stand very close.
idea.narrator: Moss, who wished for only a small warm blanket, and everyone laughed.

idea.price: Ring it eleven times and a lamp goes dark for good.
idea.title: Twelve Rings
idea.twist: The deal says twelve rings, never who rings them or how. Juno stands the whole town on the stool in turn, and every footstep, clap and stomp counts. The bell is never the only thing ringing, so the moth loses all its power over the lamps.
idea.closer: In this town, we ring twelve times every night. Now the whole square does the ringing.
idea.opener: In this town, every night we ring the square's big brass bell exactly twelve times so the Moon Moth won't eat the lamps.
idea.teaser: Twelve is the rule. Nobody read the fine print.
idea.premise: Twelve rings a night keep the Moon Moth from eating the town's lamps, and the narrator is the kid who rings the bell, until the moth shows up early and the clapper snaps.
examples: Mrs. Plum counts out loud and still loses track of eleven.
The baker bakes twelve loaves, one for every ring.
Old Mr. Tuck lost a lamp the night he sneezed.
idea.narrator: Juno, the bell ringer's kid, who is too short to reach the rope without a stool.

idea.price: Anyone who sneezes again gets one more pet, and the street is running out of room.
idea.title: The Sneeze Pet
idea.twist: A hundred pets run wild across the street. I tickle everyone's nose with the feather duster, so they sneeze again, and each new pet is a tiny, polite hamster. The wild pets vanish when their owners sneeze.
idea.closer: Everyone here got a magnificent pet. But now, when they sneeze, they call me.
idea.opener: In this town, everyone gets a random pet the moment they sneeze for the first time.
idea.teaser: Too many pets are causing chaos. One sneeze fixes it.
idea.premise: On Maple Court, a sneeze brings a pet, and I got a sad, damp sock puppet when I sneezed, while neighbours got dragons and ponies.
examples: Mr. Ruiz sneezed and got a bear who now does his taxes.
Mrs. Vale got a unicorn that eats only her tulips.
The mailman got eleven ducks and a very stern goose.
idea.narrator: A kid who got a damp sock puppet while everyone else got something magnificent.

idea.prop: A rule book of town laws
idea.price: Skip a story and the worm wiggles up and eats the street's doorsteps by morning.
idea.title: The Worm Wants Sequels
idea.twist: The law says the worm must hear a story every night, never that it must be a good one. Tobin reads the stuttery rule itself, 'every night, every night, every night,' and the worm happily falls asleep to the loop.
idea.closer: Now every night at eight, we read the worm the same line, and it begs for more.
idea.opener: In this town, every night at eight, we read one bedtime story aloud to the Hush Worm under the cave floor.
idea.teaser: The worm demands a story. Tobin only knows one sentence.
idea.premise: An underground town reads a nightly story to a giant worm that sleeps under their houses, and the town's worst storyteller is out of stories.
examples: Mrs. Pell reads recipes, and the worm gets very hungry.
The mayor read the phone book once. His porch is still missing.
Mr. Gurney does all the voices, even the furniture's.
idea.narrator: Tobin, who stutters, can't finish a sentence, and got picked to read tonight.

idea.price: Miss Hobb forgot her soup once. The wind took her roof and her chickens.
idea.title: Soup for the Wind
idea.twist: The Wind Giant is lonely and can't hear the pretty songs, because they sound like wind. Only Pim's squawky voice reaches him, so he sings back, and the Giant joins the dinner every night after that.
idea.closer: In this town, we feed the wind soup. Now it stays for dinner, and Pim sings.
idea.opener: In this town, every night each cliff house sets out one bowl of warm soup on the ledge for the Wind Giant.
idea.teaser: Everyone mocked his singing. The Giant has waited for it.
idea.premise: A cliff town feeds the Wind Giant soup every night, and the kid who sings off-key is the only one the Giant will listen to.
examples: Mr. Banks makes pea soup, and the wind always hums.
Mrs. Lark makes tomato soup, and the wind turns pink.
The bakers make bread soup, and the wind sneezes crumbs.
idea.narrator: Pim, who sings so off-key that everyone covers their ears and calls him Squawk.

idea.price: Farmer Gus counted his ducks at midnight. Now he has fourteen ducks and a goat doing his taxes.
idea.title: The Tally Goat
idea.twist: The Tally Goat only comes to the counting and must finish whatever number it is told. Bea counts to infinity out loud, and the goat, bound by the rule to check every number, trots after her until sunrise and gives up, bleating.
idea.closer: Nobody may count the chickens after dark. Except me, until the goat falls asleep.
idea.opener: In this town, nobody may count the chickens after dark, or the Tally Goat comes to check your math.
idea.teaser: The goat has to check every number. Every single one.
idea.premise: On a farm where counting is banned at night, a sleepy farm kid has to count to stay awake and keep the chickens safe.
examples: Mrs. Plum labels her hens Hen, Also Hen and Another Hen.
The cow tells time by mooing at the clock.
Mr. Dill says he owns many pigs, roughly.
idea.narrator: Bea, a farm kid who cannot fall asleep without counting, and always counts out loud.

idea.price: A grumbling stomach shakes the street and everyone's teeth rattle until breakfast.
idea.title: Pancake for the Stomach
idea.twist: The deal says 'one whole pancake on the tongue,' so Tilly serves the giant pan itself, pancake stuck on it. The walrus swallows the pan, can't grumble, and burps out a daily free breakfast.
idea.closer: In this town, every night we give the Great Stomach a pancake. Now it gives us breakfast.
idea.opener: In this town, every night we give the Great Stomach one whole pancake, stacked on the tongue, so it won't grumble.
idea.teaser: The rule said pancake. It never said how big.
idea.premise: The whole town lives inside a giant sleepy walrus, and the kid in charge of the nightly pancake has just run out of syrup and flour.
idea.setting: inside something giant (an animal, a store, a tower)
examples: Mrs. Plum flips the pancake with a tennis racket every night.
Mr. Dandy once offered a rice cake and got hiccuped into the attic.
The mayor's pancake has a tiny hat on it for luck.
idea.narrator: Tilly, the pancake kid, who can only cook things that are flat and burnt.

idea.price: Kids with silent hands get passed over for parade spots, prize ribbons, and the front row.
idea.title: No Clap
idea.twist: On market day Juno loses the parade spot, the prize ribbon, then her seat. Then a storm hits and the town's clapping roars so loud nobody hears the lost kids. Juno's silent hands let her hear their cries, and her bell guides them home.
idea.closer: Everyone here gets applause. But when the storm comes, they follow my little bell home.
idea.opener: In this town, everyone has tiny floating hands that clap whenever they do something good, except me.
idea.teaser: When the whole town got too loud, her silence mattered.
idea.premise: Everyone in the square gets applause from their own floating hands, but Juno's hands never clap, and her little handbell is the only thing that ever makes a sound for her.
examples: Baker Odell gets a standing ovation for toasting bread.
Mrs. Vane's hands clap so hard her hat falls off.
Mayor Pruitt's hands clap before he even opens his mouth.
idea.narrator: Juno, the only kid whose hands stay silent, so she rings a little handbell the town laughs at.

idea.price: Last week the Warden swallowed Mr. Fin's bright lamp, and only his boots floated back.
idea.title: Outside the Lamp
idea.twist: The Warden swallows only the biggest, brightest lights, which is why it took Mr. Fin's lamp. Nori's faint glow slips past unseen and leads the lost sub home. The bright lamps were the bait all along.
idea.closer: Everyone here fears the dark. Now they follow the dimmest light in the sea.
idea.opener: In this town, anything outside the light of a window lamp after dark belongs to the Tide Warden.
idea.teaser: The big lights draw it in. Her small one doesn't.
idea.premise: A submarine town lives by lamplight, and tiny Nori, who owns only a weak flashlight, must find a lost sub as the big lamps start going out.
examples: Captain Bell's dinner goes cold because her lamp is by the door.
Mr. Fin sleeps with his nose pressed to the glass.
Mail Eel Gus only swims between two lamps, never three.
idea.narrator: Nori, the smallest kid, mocked for her pocket flashlight that glows weaker than a birthday candle.

idea.price: Short-box kids wait until dark, and some letters never reach them.
idea.title: The Short Mailbox
idea.twist: The storm floods the street and the tall boxes tip and wash away, but Nell's low shoebox sits firm. She gathers every letter in it, and the whole street lines up at her little box.
idea.closer: Everyone here wanted the tallest mailbox. Now they all line up at mine.
idea.opener: In this town, kids with tall mailboxes are Highs who get the mail first, and kids with short mailboxes wait at the curb.
idea.teaser: When the storm blows, small stays standing.
idea.premise: A street ranks everyone by mailbox height, and the narrator's mailbox is the shortest on the block when a storm threatens every letter in town.
examples: Mrs. Vane's mailbox is so tall it needs a ladder.
The Highs get fresh letters every morning.
Our mailbox is so low that the dog sleeps on top.
idea.narrator: Nell, whose mailbox is a shoebox on a stick, and the postman skips it.

idea.price: Anyone who lives above the Diggers must carry their rubble and their rules.
idea.title: The Shallow Kid
idea.twist: When the deep tunnels flood, the Bottom Diggers' own rule says the highest-ranked person leads the escape. Nell digs her house down, then up through the roof, so deepest becomes the way out.
idea.closer: In this town, the deeper you dig, the higher you rank. So I dug up.
idea.opener: In this town, the deeper your house is dug, the higher your rank, so the Bottom Diggers give all the orders.
idea.teaser: The shallow kid has a shovel and a very strange idea.
idea.premise: In a cave town ruled by whoever lives deepest, Nell lives in a shallow hole by the entrance and discovers the rank-keeper's rule has a loophole that could save everyone.
examples: Mrs. Gruff lives nine floors down and gets her soup delivered.
The mail carrier bows to every mailbox below the lamp line.
Mr. Tink dug an extra cellar and now bosses the baker.
idea.narrator: Nell, whose family house is the shallowest hole in town, right by the cave mouth.

idea.prop: A joke book with one torn page
idea.price: Last time the joke was bad, the Echo repeated it for a week and nobody slept.
idea.title: Joke Night
idea.twist: The deal says the Echo repeats whatever it is given forever. Biscuit gives it the worst joke ever written, so it repeats it and the Echo can never say another thing, and the town can finally sleep.
idea.closer: In this town, we give the Echo one joke each night. Mine was the last one.
idea.opener: In this town, every night we give the Cave Echo one joke, and it promises to laugh politely.
idea.teaser: The deal said it repeats every joke forever. Biscuit chose carefully.
idea.premise: The cave town pays the Echo a joke every night, and Biscuit, the kid with the worst jokes, has to deliver it when the town runs out.
examples: Mr. Pebble told the one about the rock and the Echo said it forty times.
The baker pays in puns, and the whole bakery groans.
The mayor tells knock-knock jokes with nobody ever answering.
idea.narrator: Biscuit, a kid whose jokes are so bad even his dog leaves the room.

idea.price: The Millers' lantern went missing once. Next morning half their fence was walking away on its own.
idea.title: The Hollow King's Promise
idea.twist: The deal says the King won't cross the fence. Juniper moves the fence inward, so the whole town stands outside and the King is stuck on the far side, trapped by his own promise.
idea.closer: The King keeps his promise perfectly. He just never noticed who moved the fence.
idea.opener: In this town, every family leaves one lantern at the woods edge every night, and the Hollow King promises not to cross the line.
idea.teaser: He promised never to cross the line. Who draws the line?
idea.premise: A town pays the Hollow King a lantern each night for a promise never to cross the fence, but tonight the lanterns are all gone.
examples: Old Mr. Quill keeps a spare lantern in the freezer.
The Millers lost theirs once. Half their fence walked off.
The mayor counts all lanterns twice with a clipboard.
idea.narrator: Juniper, a fence painter's kid who reads every word of the town's contracts.

idea.prop: A little brass gate counting bell
idea.price: Anyone whose breath number fades below one is left outside the gate.
idea.title: Zero Breath
idea.twist: The gate rule says the gate opens only for 'a number'. Everyone's numbers freeze and fall in the blizzard, but Juno's zero never fades, so she rings the bell and zero opens the gate for the whole lost team.
idea.closer: Everyone here breathes out a number. But when the storm comes, they wait for my zero.
idea.opener: In this town, everyone's breath freezes into a number in the air, and the bigger your number, the louder the town cheers.
idea.teaser: Her number was the one thing the storm couldn't erase.
idea.premise: In a snowy town ruled by breath numbers, the narrator's breath never shows anything, and now a blizzard has trapped the whole town's sled team on the mountain.
examples: Mayor Tilly's breath says 98 and she never lets anyone forget.
Baker Odo's breath fell to 3 last winter, so now he sleeps in the shed.
The twins trade breath numbers like cards at recess.
idea.narrator: Juno, whose breath shows a blank zero, which the gate rule says doesn't count as a number at all.

idea.price: Anyone who walks into the woods without a lantern is lost until morning.
idea.title: No Lantern Me
idea.twist: When a fog rolls in, every lantern glare turns the woods into a white wall. Moss's glasses, no glare at all, let him see the path, so he leads everyone home one hand at a time.
idea.closer: Everyone here has a lantern at the woods edge. Now they all hold on to me.
idea.opener: In this town, everyone at the woods edge is born with a glowing lantern floating at their shoulder, except me.
idea.teaser: When the fog came, the brightest lights were the blind ones.
idea.premise: Everyone near the woods edge has a floating lantern that lights their way, and one kid with none is laughed at and left behind on evening walks.
examples: Mr. Birch's lantern sings off-key and he claps along.
The twins' lanterns argue about who shines brighter.
Baker Ash uses his lantern as a very bright oven.
idea.narrator: Moss, who has no lantern and wears a pair of big round glasses everyone teases.

idea.price: Skip the cocoa and the drain steams, and the house above it is gone by morning.
idea.title: The Frost Drinker
idea.twist: The law says the Frost Drinker sleeps only while the drain is fed, never what it is fed. Tilly ladles in snow and the cold wakes it, so it follows the drain's rule and drinks all the snow forever, never rising.
idea.closer: Every night we still pour cocoa. But now it's the Frost Drinker who stays up for ours.
idea.opener: In this town, every family pours one pot of hot cocoa into the snow drain every night, so the Frost Drinker stays asleep.
idea.teaser: Nobody ever asked what the drain actually needs.
idea.premise: A snowy town keeps a giant sleeper under the street calm with nightly cocoa, and the narrator's family has just run out of cocoa powder.
examples: Mrs. Lund stirs her cocoa forty times, never thirty-nine.
The baker sells marshmallows only to people with full pots.
Mr. Orrin once poured tea. His chimney is still missing.
idea.narrator: Tilly, the youngest, whose job is to carry the family ladle and always spills a little.
